title: How they say it there
job: Regional and generational speech; what marks an outsider
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: N-nom + Adj-nom + sum (one spelling, three traditions in sound)

rules.text: FOR LATIN, 'HOW THEY SAY IT THERE' IS NOT A PLACE — IT IS A TRADITION. There is no home vernacular and there has not been for centuries, so this module cannot be about a region. What Latin has instead is THREE LIVING PRONUNCIATION TRADITIONS: restored classical (c always k, v as w, ae as 'eye'), ecclesiastical (c as ch before e and i, v as v, ae as 'ay'), and the national school traditions, of which the English one is the strangest. Cicerō is KEE-ke-roh, CHEE-che-roh or SISS-er-oh depending on who is reading, and all three are reading the same six letters.

display STAYS IN THIS COURSE's TRADITION AND sound IS WHERE THE VARIANTS LIVE. One sentence, one spelling, and a sound line naming what each tradition does with it — which is why nothing in this module changes the emitted index and no key is spent on a variant. docs/123's macrons are this course's ORTHOGRAPHY and not a claim about pronunciation: every tradition keeps the vowel lengths and differs on the consonants. An author who writes two displays for two traditions has minted two keys for one sentence.

THE REGISTER SPECTRUM RUNS A THOUSAND YEARS AND IT IS WHAT ACTUALLY MARKS AN OUTSIDER. Plautine is short and coordinate; Ciceronian subordinates; Vulgar lets prepositions do what endings did. S05 and S06 are the SAME CONTENT at two levels, and nothing in the higher one is new grammar — L3-M2's relative and L3-M3's pointing word. What marks a learner is not accent but LEVEL: a relative clause in a joke, or tandem in a funeral oration.

cīvis IS A TWO-SHAPE WORD LIKE L2-M2's fortis, and its nominative and genitive are identical — so cīvis looks like a form that could do anything, and its object is cīvem. This module keeps two of its plates on that shape rather than on pronunciation, because a module about how a language sounds still has to be a module about Latin.

dē IS THE SEAM OF VULGAR LATIN, AND IT IS ORDINARY CLASSICAL USAGE TOO. dē patriā dīcō is 'I speak about my homeland' and Cicero would write it. But dē is also the word that ate the case system: where classical Latin used an ending, later Latin put dē in front, and French de, Spanish de and Italian di are all this word. A learner who has met any Romance language has already met it — and dē takes the ABLATIVE, which after thirty-nine modules of ad plus an object shape is the reflex to resist.

THE REGISTERS ARE NOT SEALED OFF FROM EACH OTHER. Anybody's Latin moves between them mid-sentence, and S09 has a Plautine question with a classical preposition in it. What marks an outsider is not mixing them but mixing them WRONGLY — and that judgement is the one thing in this module a dictionary cannot supply.

A MOTTO OR A STANDARD TAKES THE IMPERFECT, which M1 of this level established for Augustus and this module reuses for Cicero: ita Cicerō dīcēbat, 'so Cicero used to say'. L4-M8 opened that tense thirty-four modules after L1-M5 deferred it, and attribution is the second job it has turned out to do.

words.note: 'Citizen' — cīvis as the subject, cīvem as the object. Same shape for a man or a woman, like L2-M2's fortis. English 'civil' and 'city' come from it.
'Roman' — L1-M1's adjective, agreeing with cīvis. rōmānus for a man, rōmāna for a woman.
'I am' — sum, es, est, sunt. L1-M1's verb, and the first word this course ever taught.

sentences.trap: ONE SPELLING, THREE PRONUNCIATIONS, AND THE display DOES NOT MOVE. A restored-classical reader says KEE-wis roh-MAH-nus; an ecclesiastical reader says CHEE-vis roh-MAH-nus; an English school reader says SIGH-vis roh-MAY-nus. Same letters, same macrons, three traditions — and this course's spelling is an ORTHOGRAPHY, not a claim about any of them.
sentences.sound: Restored classical: KEE-wis roh-MAH-noos SOOM — c is always k, v is w, u is oo. Ecclesiastical: CHEE-vis roh-MAH-noos — c before i is ch, v is v. English school tradition: SIGH-vis roh-MAY-nus. The macrons mark LENGTH and every tradition keeps them.

words.note: 'Citizen' — cīvis as the subject, cīvem as the object. Same shape for a man or a woman, like L2-M2's fortis. English 'civil' and 'city' come from it.
'Who' — L3-M2's relative pronoun, masculine subject. The course writes three of its five shapes.
'Homeland' — literally 'the fatherland', from pater. patria as the subject, patriam as the object.
'He sees' — videō, vidēs, videt.
'From, about' plus the ablative — and it is the seam of Vulgar Latin: where a classical writer used a case ending, later Latin put dē in front, and every Romance language is built on that change.
'It' after dē — the feminine ablative of is, ea, id, whose object eum L3-M3 opened. It points back at patria.
'He says, he speaks' — dīcō, dīcis, dīcit.

sentences.trap: THE SAME CONTENT AS S05, AT A HIGHER LEVEL. A relative clause inside the subject, a pronoun pointing back — this is the Ciceronian end, and nothing in it is new: L3-M2 taught the relative and L3-M3 the pointing word. What marks a register is how much subordination a speaker is willing to build, and a learner writing this in a conversation is as marked as one writing S05 in a letter.
sentences.sound: Restored classical: KEE-wis, kwee PA-tri-am WI-det, day E-ah DEE-kit. Ecclesiastical: CHEE-vis, kwee PA-tri-am VEE-det, day E-ah DEE-chit — dīcit's c IS before i, so here it does become ch.

sentences.trap: dē twice, where a classical writer would have used one case ending and no preposition at all. THIS IS WHAT VULGAR LATIN LOOKS LIKE from the inside: prepositions doing the work endings used to do, repeated because they are cheap. Nobody wrote this on purpose; everybody drifted towards it, and Romance is where it arrived.
sentences.sound: Restored classical: day KEE-we day PA-tri-ah DEE-koh. Say it twice and you can hear why the endings stopped mattering: the preposition is carrying the sense and the ending is just a habit.

mistake.why: two object shapes after two prepositions that want the ablative. The sentence is already a drift towards Romance, and putting the wrong case in it is the drift arriving: once dē is carrying the sense, the ending stops feeling load-bearing — which is exactly how the case system went.

words.note: 'Citizen' — cīvis as the subject, cīvem as the object. Same shape for a man or a woman, like L2-M2's fortis. English 'civil' and 'city' come from it.
'Roman' — L1-M1's adjective, agreeing with cīvis.
'I am' — sum, es, est, sunt.
'So'. L1-M2's word, pointing back at the quotation.
The orator whose prose is the standard this course calls Ciceronian. A Roman name in the subject shape.
'He used to say' — L4-M8's imperfect of dīcō. M1 of this level used the same shape for Augustus's motto: a thing somebody said repeatedly.

sentences.trap: Cicero's own sentence, and the man the register is named after. Cīvis Rōmānus sum was a formula that got a Roman out of trouble anywhere in the empire, and it is three words — which is worth noticing in a module about register, because the most famous Ciceronian sentence is not a Ciceronian period at all.
sentences.sound: Restored classical: KEE-ke-roh — both c's are k, which is why the English 'SISS-er-oh' is a school tradition and not a reconstruction. Ecclesiastical: CHEE-che-roh. Italian says Cicerone the ecclesiastical way, and that is the same tradition.

The registers are not sealed off from each other — a speaker moves between them mid-sentence — and what marks an outsider is not mixing them but mixing them wrongly: tandem in a funeral oration, or a relative clause in a joke.

sentences.sound: Restored classical throughout: KEE-wis SOOM; day PA-tri-ah DEE-koh. KEE-wis, kwee PA-tri-am WI-det, day E-ah DEE-kit: I-ta KEE-ke-roh dee-KAY-bat.
